query: For bulk HfNbTaTiZr, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified predictive approach make to overcome the limited accuracy of available analytical predictions and their usual restriction to perfect, defect-free crystals? Address the nearly 0–200 K regime and the 300–1200 K regime, for which measurements also exist on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen; explain why the approach should improve accuracy, predict its advantage over existing analytical approaches, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a held-out conductivity benchmark and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: An ML‐enhanced predictive framework that uses actively learned moment tensor potentials (MTPs) to explicitly include oxygen‐induced defects and local atomic relaxations in bulk HfNbTaTiZr will yield accurate low‐frequency conductivity predictions across both the cryogenic regime (0–200 K) and the elevated-temperature regime (300–1200 K). This improvement arises from explicitly capturing the oxygen-induced defect scattering and local atomic relaxations that play a crucial role in electron transport in this multi-principal-element alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: Bulk equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr produced by standard synthesis methods, with one set of specimens containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen (as a representative impurity level) and another as near-pristine.
generation.intervention: Implementation of a computational framework that integrates active learning with MTPs to simulate large supercells including explicitly modeled oxygen-induced defects and local structural distortions.
generation.conditions: Simulations and experiments conducted over two temperature regimes – cryogenic (0–200 K) and elevated (300–1200 K) – with samples both with and without ~1 wt.% oxygen.
generation.structural_mediator: Local atomic relaxations and defect clusters triggered by oxygen incorporation, as well as potential short-range clustering and microstructural inhomogeneities that influence electron scattering.
generation.mechanism: By training the MTP on configurations that include defects and local relaxation effects, the model captures scattering phenomena and electronic structure variations that impact conductivity. This enables the prediction of temperature-dependent conductivity that reflects both phonon and defect (impurity) scattering, unlike traditional analytical models that assume ideal lattices.
generation.predicted_outcome: The ML-enhanced model will predict low-frequency conductivity values within approximately ±30% of experimental measurements across both temperature regimes. In particular, oxygen-doped (1 wt.%) specimens will show a modest but reproducible reduction in conductivity at cryogenic temperatures compared to defect-free predictions, while at higher temperatures phonon contributions dominate and the predictions converge closer to experimental values.
generation.baseline: Existing analytical predictions based on perfect, defect-free crystals typically show large errors (sometimes an order-of-magnitude discrepancy) when applied to real samples with defects and oxygen impurities.
generation.boundary: The approach is applicable to bulk, equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr with oxygen levels up to about 1 wt.% and for temperatures ranging from 0 K to 1200 K. Extremely high impurity levels or severe phase alterations (beyond moderate oxygen contamination) may lie outside the model’s current calibration.
generation.uncertainty: The exact percentage improvement in quantitative conductivity predictions is uncertain due to limited training data for defect configurations and varied oxygen incorporation effects; the ±30% target is an estimate based on similar ML-enhanced methodologies applied to complex alloys.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of bulk HfNbTaTiZr samples: one nearly pristine and one doped with ~1 wt.% oxygen. Measure the low-frequency electrical conductivity at several temperatures within the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes using techniques such as terahertz spectroscopy and four-point probe measurements. In parallel, perform ML-enhanced simulations that include oxygen-induced defect configurations and compare the predicted conductivity values to the experimental data.
measurements: Electrical conductivity at selected temperatures (e.g., 100 K, 300 K, 800 K, 1200 K)
Microstructural characterization (e.g., defect density, local relaxations via TEM/XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the predicted conductivity values from the ML-enhanced model do not fall within ±30% of the experimental measurements across both temperature regimes, or if the oxygen-doped samples do not exhibit the predicted reduction in conductivity (especially at cryogenic temperatures) relative to the near-pristine samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

In conclusion, we have demonstrated how a combination of CPA and actively-learned MTPs can solve the problem of predicting the CRSS and intrinsic ductility of refractory MPEAs over the whole composition space with ab initio accuracy, a problem that is currently not tractable with conventional ab initio-based methods. In particular, by integrating our ab initio automated workflow into a robust Bayesian multi-objective optimization framework we have applied the developed approach to identifying high-performance Pareto-optimal compositions. Furthermore, our supercell size convergence tests enabled by MTP-powered molecular statics have revealed that sizes of typical supercell sizes used in conventional SQS calculations are often insufficient for accurate calculations of certain important materials properties, such as the surface energy, of multi-component alloys. Specifically, the surface energy of MoNbTi has been shown to exhibit a rather slow convergence with the supercell size, which leads to errors of 10–20% for SQS supercells of about 100 atoms.

cited_evidence.kind: web:3.4.2. Monte Carlo Simulation of Microstructure
cited_evidence.text: Ab-initio MC simulation was performed to evaluate the microstructure stability of investigated alloys. Simulation was performed for the 5 element HfNbTaTiZr alloy, because it contains all elements considered in investigated alloys. Hf, Nb, Ta, Ti, Zr ions were distributed randomly in equimolar concentration into a 250 atom BCC supercell. This initial state was relaxed with respect to ion positions until minimum of the total free energy was reached. The equilibrium configuration corresponding to minimum free energy was obtained using a Metropolis MC algorithm at 300 K (room temperature). The details of the simulation and more complete results will be published elsewhere. Figure 7 shows the equilibrium atomic configuration corresponding to the minimum of total energy. The most apparent effect is a rather one-dimensional Ta object (‘wire’) along the <100> direction. The Ta wire is surrounded predominantly by Nb ions. The rest of the simulation box is filled up by the mixture of Ti, Zr and Hf. The latter two elements appear to be well separated from the Ta and Nb region.
